metaDescription: Seven Tiger rice cookers from 3 to 10 cups, split between micom models with the tacook tray and simple one-button cookers, with real tradeoffs for each.
expertTake: The Tiger JBV-A10U 5.5 Cup micom cooker is the best pick for most homes because it adds microcomputer control and the tacook tray at a family size. The Tiger JNP-S10U-KY 5.5 Cup is the value pick for anyone who only wants rice from a simple one-button cooker. Anyone who cooks rice once a week should skip the 10 cup models, which are wasteful for small batches.
introParagraphs: This maker sells two clearly different types of cooker. One group uses a microcomputer to manage the cooking stages, and the other is a conventional style with a single push button and a thermostat. Both cook rice, but the first gives more control over texture and the second gives a lower price and almost nothing to go wrong.

The sensible way to choose is by how you cook. A micom model suits people who want brown rice, porridge or a rice and main dish cooked together. A conventional model suits people who want white rice on demand. This guide compares seven cookers across both groups using the listing specs and standard rice cooker engineering, with attention to capacity, keep-warm limits and cleanup.

products.name: Tiger JBV-A10U 5.5 Cup Micom Rice Cooker with Tacook Tray

specList.label: Feature
specList.value: Cooks rice and a main dish together

products.description:
The JBV-A10U is the sweet spot of the range. A microcomputer controls the cooking stages, and the tacook tray sits above the rice so a main dish cooks at the same time. The listing describes synchronized cooking that finishes rice and dish together, which saves a pot and a burner on a weeknight.

The tradeoff is complexity. The tray adds a part to wash, and a marinated protein over the rice requires you to plan the timing and portion sizes. Compared with the JNP-S10U-KY it costs more and does more, but if you only cook plain rice you are paying for features you will not use. Compared with the 10 cup JBV-A18U it is easier to store and fits a family of four.

Ownership is routine. Wash the inner pot and tray after each use, wipe the steam vent and keep the heating plate dry. A micom model adjusts cooking length and temperature automatically, which means it is less likely to scorch rice than a basic thermostat unit.  Because the tray sits above the rice, steam from the rice also warms the dish, which is why the timing works without a second heater.
products.bestFor: Families who want micom control and a rice-plus-dish tray at a mid size.

5.5 cup capacity suits four to five people
cons: Tray adds a part to wash

products.name: Tiger JBV-A18U 10 Cup Micom Rice Cooker with Tacook Tray
products.description:
The JBV-A18U is the large micom model. It combines microcomputer control with the tacook tray and adds a slow-cook function. A 10 cup capacity feeds a big family or a gathering, and the listing says the tray is BPA-free.

The tradeoff is size and cost. A 10 cup cooker is heavy and takes counter space, and small batches in a large pot can scorch the bottom. It is also the most expensive Tiger in this guide. Compared with the JBV-A10U it gives about twice the volume but cooks small amounts less gracefully.

Use the slow-cook mode for stews, noting that a rice cooker's slow cook is gentler than a dedicated slow cooker. Wash the tray, pot and lid after each use. It suits large households that cook rice daily. Because it is so large, check that your counter has headroom for the lid when it swings open and releases steam.
products.bestFor: Large families that cook rice in big batches every day.

products.name: Tiger JAX-T10U-K 5.5 Cup Micom Rice Cooker and Warmer
products.description:
The JAX-T10U-K is a 5.5 cup micom cooker and warmer. Cooking length and temperature adjust automatically, and tacook tray technology lets rice and a main dish cook together. A warmer mode keeps rice ready for serving.

The tradeoff is similarity to the JBV-A10U. Both are 5.5 cup micom cookers with a tray, so the choice comes down to styling, menus and price at the time. It is not a different class of machine. It is also still a rice cooker, so extended keep-warm will eventually dry rice.

Wash the pot and tray after each use, wipe the vent and avoid leaving rice on warm for more than a few hours. It suits cooks who want a micom model in a black finish. Because it shares so much with its sibling, buy whichever is cheaper or in the finish you prefer.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a 5.5 cup micom model with a warmer.

products.name: Tiger JNP-S15U-KY 8 Cup Conventional Rice Cooker
products.description:
The JNP-S15U-KY is a conventional cooker with a single push button, a nonstick inner pot, a retractable power cord and a keep-warm that lasts up to 12 hours. Eight cups uncooked feeds a large family. There is almost no learning curve: add rice and water, press the button and walk away.

The tradeoff is control. A thermostat cooker has one program, so brown rice, porridge and sushi rice are less reliable than on the micom models. Compared with the JBV-A10U it has no tray and no microcomputer, but it costs less and has fewer parts to fail.

Wash the nonstick pot with a soft sponge, wipe the steam vent and keep the heating plate dry. Do not leave rice on warm for the full 12 hours if you want it moist. It suits big families who want a simple cooker. Because rice cookers cups are 180 ml, eight cups uncooked is about 1.4 litres of dry rice by volume.
products.bestFor: Large households that cook white rice and want a simple cooker.
cons: Single program, weak on brown rice

products.name: Tiger JNP-S10U-KY 5.5 Cup Conventional Rice Cooker
products.description:
The JNP-S10U-KY is the straightforward family cooker. It has single push-button operation, a nonstick inner pot, a retractable cord and keep-warm up to 12 hours. At 5.5 cups it feeds four to five people with room for leftovers.

With a single program, it is not the machine for brown rice or porridge. Compared with the JBV-A10U it has no microcomputer and no tray. Compared with the 8 cup JNP-S15U-KY it holds less but stores more easily.

Rinse the rice, use the marked water line and wash the pot gently. White rice done reliably, with no payment for features, is the whole proposition. Because it is so simple, it is also the model that least often needs a repair or a spare part.
products.bestFor: Families who want reliable white rice at the lowest cost in the range.

products.name: Tiger JNP-S55U-KY 3 Cup Conventional Rice Cooker
products.description:
The JNP-S55U-KY is the small version of the conventional cooker. It has one push button, a nonstick pot, a retractable cord and keep-warm up to 12 hours. Three cups uncooked is enough for one to three people.

The tradeoff is capacity. A 3 cup cooker makes about six cups cooked, which suits a couple but not a family. Compared with the JNP-S10U-KY it takes less counter space and cooks small batches better, since a large pot scorches thin batches.

Wash gently and keep the heating plate dry. It suits singles and couples who cook white rice most days. Because it is small, it also suits a dorm, an office or a boat where space is tight.
products.bestFor: Singles and couples who want a compact one-button cooker.

products.name: Tiger JAZ-A18U-LF 10 Cup Conventional Rice Cooker
products.description:
The JAZ-A18U-LF is a 10 cup conventional cooker with a single push button, a nonstick pot and a retractable cord. Up to 10 cups of dried rice fit in a single batch. It is built for big households and gatherings.

The tradeoff is the same as every conventional model: one program and no micom control. A large pot with a small batch can scorch, and brown rice is not its strength. Compared with the JBV-A18U it costs less and has no tray.

Wash the nonstick pot with a soft sponge and keep the vent clear. It suits big families that cook white rice every day. Because it holds up to 10 cups of dried rice, consider whether you really need that much before buying.
products.bestFor: Big households and gatherings that want a simple large cooker.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Micom models like the JBV-A10U, JBV-A18U and JAX-T10U-K use a microcomputer to adjust cooking length and temperature. Conventional models like the JNP-S10U-KY use one thermostat and one button. Micom gives better results with brown rice and porridge, while conventional gives a lower price and almost nothing to fail. Choose by how varied your rice cooking is. The practical test is whether you ever cook brown rice, porridge or mixed grains, because that is where the micom control earns its price.

The tacook tray lets you cook a main dish above the rice at the same time. It saves a pot and a burner, but it adds a part to wash and requires you to plan the portion. If you cook plain rice and a separate main, you will not use it. If you cook weeknight one-pot meals, it is the main reason to buy a micom Tiger. A bamboo or silicone rack is a cheap alternative if you only need steaming occasionally.

A 3 cup cooker like the JNP-S55U-KY makes six cups cooked, a 5.5 cup cooker feeds four to five and the 8 and 10 cup models feed a large household. Rice cooker cups are 180 ml, not US cups. Cooking a small batch in a large pot scorches the bottom, so buy for your usual meal. If your batch is always small, resist the temptation to buy the largest pot just because it is cheap per cup.

Conventional models list keep-warm up to 12 hours, but rice dries and yellows well before that. For moist rice, serve within a few hours or refrigerate leftovers. Micom models adjust warming a little more gently, but no cooker keeps rice fresh overnight. Fluff the rice right after cooking to let steam escape, which keeps it from clumping.

All the Tiger models here use nonstick inner pots. Use the supplied paddle, avoid metal and scouring pads, and wash soon after cooking. A scratched coating sticks and flakes, which is the usual reason a cooker is replaced after several years. Rinsing the rice gently also reduces the starch that causes sticking.

A retractable cord helps storage on conventional models. A tray or tacook plate adds washing. Wipe the steam vent and the heating plate regularly, since starch residue and stray grains cause odors and uneven heating. Check the manual for which parts are dishwasher safe. Wipe the lid gasket regularly, since stray grains can lodge there and break the seal.

specDecoder.watchFor: The JNP-S10U-KY lists 5.5 cups and the JAZ-A18U-LF lists 10 cups.

specDecoder.meaning: The maximum holding time, not the time rice stays good.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control type
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared micom and conventional models for brown rice, porridge and consistency. We also noted which models offer menus beyond white rice.

howWeEvaluated.title: Feature value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the tacook tray against its added cleaning and planning. A tray is only valuable if you will use it at least weekly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity spread
howWeEvaluated.description: We covered 3, 5.5, 8 and 10 cup models, mapped to household sizes. We also weighed storage footprint, since a 10 cup cooker is a counter commitment.

howWeEvaluated.title: Keep-warm behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted the 12 hour listing and the real limit on rice freshness. No model here is recommended for overnight warming of rice.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at nonstick pots, cords and removable parts. Cord and handle design also counted toward ease of storage.

faq.q: What is the difference between micom and conventional Tiger cookers?
faq.a: Micom models adjust cooking time and temperature automatically and add the tacook tray. Conventional models use one thermostat and one button, and cost less. For most households the choice comes down to whether you cook more than white rice.

faq.q: Is the tacook tray worth it?
faq.a: If you cook one-pot meals, yes. It lets you cook a main dish above the rice. If you cook plain rice, it adds washing.

faq.q: How long can rice stay on keep warm?
faq.a: The models list up to 12 hours, but rice dries and yellows long before that. Aim for a few hours. Spread leftover rice thinly and refrigerate it within a couple of hours.
A 3 cup suits one to three people, a 5.5 cup suits four to five and 8 to 10 cups suit large households.
Micom models handle it better. Conventional cookers can cook it but with less control, so expect to adjust water. Rinse the rice and use the brown rice water line if the cooker has one.
Check the manual. Hand washing with a soft sponge protects the nonstick coating. A soft sponge and warm water are enough.
